title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)
intro: Obsessive-compulsive disorder involves unwanted, distressing thoughts, images or urges called obsessions, and repetitive behaviours or mental acts called compulsions performed to reduce the distress. It is far more than being tidy or particular. OCD can take up much time and cause suffering, but cognitive behavioural therapy and medicine are effective.

sections.heading: What OCD looks like
paragraphs: Common obsessions include fear of contamination, doubts about having locked the door or turned off appliances, intrusive aggressive or sexual thoughts, and a need for symmetry. Compulsions include excessive washing, checking, counting, repeating and mental rituals. People usually recognise the thoughts as excessive but feel unable to stop.

sections.heading: Causes
paragraphs: OCD arises from a combination of genetic, brain and environmental factors. It often begins in childhood or young adulthood and can be worsened by stress. It is not caused by weak character or poor upbringing. Depression, anxiety and tics often occur alongside it.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: Diagnosis is made through a conversation with a doctor or psychotherapist, who asks about the nature and time spent on obsessions and compulsions and how they interfere with life. Many people wait years before seeking help because of shame, so early treatment is encouraged.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention is the first-choice psychological treatment. The person is gradually exposed to feared situations and learns to resist rituals, so that anxiety fades over time. Antidepressants, especially selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often at higher doses, help many people and may be combined with therapy.
For severe cases that do not respond, specialist options such as intensive programmes are available.

sections.heading: Living with OCD
paragraphs: Avoid reassurance seeking and accommodating rituals, which can maintain the problem, and involve family in understanding. Self-help books and support groups can complement treatment.

examples.title: Seeking help
examples.text: Imagine you spend hours checking the stove each morning. You could write down how much time it takes, tell your doctor and ask for referral to a therapist experienced in exposure therapy.

examples.title: Supporting a relative
examples.text: Suppose a family member keeps asking you to confirm that things are clean. You might talk with the therapist about how to respond kindly without feeding the compulsion.
